France’s government faces a deepening political test after nationwide protests over living costs and public services descended into the country’s worst unrest in years. Around 550,000 people marched on Saturday, with almost 2,400 arrested and nearly 1,000 police officers injured. Rioters attacked public buildings and shops. At the same time many demonstrators protested peacefully but found their peaceful protests hijacked by rioters and looters. ... US President Donald Trump has endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the October 27 election, praising his leadership during the joint US-Israeli war against Iran. Trump also suggested further American action against Iran could depend on Netanyahu remaining in office, saying he was reluctant to act alone under another Israeli leader. ... Saudi Arabia’s advanced military is struggling to contain Houthi missile and drone attacks, exposing weaknesses in its air defences despite one of the world’s largest defence budgets. A strike on Riyadh’s international airport killed at least 13 people, while another attack injured six in Najran on Sunday. Saudi officials face shortages of missile interceptors and the challenge of protecting infrastructure spread across vast territory. ... Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign after six days of student-led protests, warning that the unrest threatens the country’s ambition to join the European Union. Demonstrations over alleged corruption, unemployment and poor education standards have spread from Tirana to other cities. Protesters have attacked government buildings, banks and shops, while police have used tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets. ... The United States has resumed intelligence sharing on Russian ballistic missile launches after a three day interruption, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday. Ukraine relies on American warnings to detect incoming missiles but alerts came only after five Russian missiles struck Kyiv on October 12. Zelensky said the service was now restored, although restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield satellite communications remain in place. ... Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a summit with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss ending the Ukraine war without Ukrainian participation. The meeting could take place alongside November’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed discussions but said neither the meeting nor its agenda had been agreed. ... The format would exclude Ukraine and European governments from discussions about the war’s settlement. China has indicated it would not object if Trump agreed, although he has not committed. The prospect has alarmed Kyiv and European allies concerned about a settlement favouring Moscow. Kenya has confirmed an eighth Ebola infection as an outbreak originating in the Democratic Republic of Congo continues to spread across East Africa. Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said one of 38 people tested on Sunday was positive. The 49-year-old patient attendant, who cleaned utensils and linens, was probably exposed to Kenya’s first case, a traveller from Congo who died in Nairobi on October 5. ... Congo has recorded at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since May. The virus has now reached eight Congolese provinces, while North Kivu authorities plan restrictions on arrivals from neighbouring Ituri. Uganda previously recorded 20 cases and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.

items.excerpt: Masked Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked Palestinians and European diplomats in the West Bank town of Taybeh who were participating in the annual olive harvest. Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khourieh said the extremists beat a Palestinian teenager, pushed an older woman, and smashed the window of a Belgian diplomatic vehicle, and that the violence “shows nobody is protected- not Palestinians, not journalists, and not diplomats.” U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor Riley Barnes, U.S. Ambassador to the Holy See Brian Burch, and other U.S. diplomats yesterday visited Taybeh. Israeli police today said they arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in the West Bank over the weekend. Aaron Boxerman and Adam Rasgon report for the New York Times; Ali Sawafta and Steven Scheer report for Reuters; Alexander Cornwell and Lili Bayer report for Reuters. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy today said Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian attack overnight that killed 3 people. Russia launched one of its broadest air assaults in months, cutting power to more than half a million households as more than 10 energy facilities were damaged. Zelenskyy yesterday announced that the United States had resumed providing Ukraine critical intelligence to help it defend against Russian missile strikes, while U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio today denied that the United States had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Olena Harmash reports for Reuters; Dan Peleschuk and Michael Derby report for Reuters; Gram Slattery reports for Reuters. Ukraine yesterday launched the biggest attack on Russian city St. Petersburg since the start of the war, killing one person and injuring another five, according to St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov. The strikes hit St. Petersburg’s oil infrastructure and the city’s airport temporarily suspended its services. Milàn Czerny reports for the Wall Street Journal. President Trump on Friday issued an executive order suspending numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect. Trump justified the suspensions by saying they were in the U.S. national interest. Zelenskyy said it was unfortunate that the United States had decided to “completely disregard” the sanctions, and later told leaders at an EU summit that it was nice to be among “real leaders.” Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Trump’s order was “an important and truly historic moment,” and that the sanctions would have inflicted “serious damage” on the United States and global market. Max Matza reports for BBC News. ... Putin has proposed that he, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet next month to talk about Ukraine in an attempt to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, sources told the Wall Street Journal. A former Russian intelligence officer said Putin floated the idea during an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions ... Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney yesterday said four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright military in Alberta on Saturday. Carney said flags across the country would fly at half-staff on federal buildings to honor those affected by the tragedy. Canadian Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said a fast moving grass fire caused the incident, and that military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was sufficiently contained to allow training to continue before winds suddenly shifted. Rob Gillies and Ty O’Neil report for AP News.

items.title: Treasury yields move lower as investors assess U.S. inflation backdrop
items.excerpt: Treasury yields moved higher on Monday as investors continue to weigh the domestic inflation and interest rate backdrop against broader geopolitical developments. The yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose more than 4 basis points to 5.146%. The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist bond yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was more than 4 basis points higher at 5.478%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note Add To Watchlist, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was up more than 3 basis points at 4.772%. ... The moves come as inflation concerns continue to loom over the U.S. economy. Last week's strong inflation data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics saw wholesale prices rise 6.3% annually last month — the biggest jump since 2022 — with consumer costs up 3.7% annually in September, beating estimates. Meanwhile, U.S. crude prices rose Monday as investors continued to weigh tensions in the Middle East, as well as those between Russia and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate futures Add To Watchlist for November delivery were up 2.22% to close at $103.66 per barrel. Brent crude Add To Watchlist, the global oil price benchmark, dropped 0.28% to $109.55, however. With the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision due Oct. 28, traders are now pricing in an above-80% probability that the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will leave borrowing costs unchanged, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

items.excerpt: Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much. ... Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%. ... Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year. ... By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks. ... Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago. ... The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones. Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.

items.title: Hassett Says CPI Data Shows Inflation Needs ‘Some Work’
items.excerpt: Enda Curran Mon, October 19, 2026 at 9:04 AM CDT 2 min read ... (Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said prices have been falling for items such as beef and eggs, though consumer price data for September shows overall inflation continues to need policy attention. "If you look at the previous three months, it looked like inflation was completely under control, and now it looks like it's sort of back needing some work," Hassett told CNBC Monday. Data last week showed consumer prices advanced in September at the fastest pace in five months and a gauge of underlying price pressures rose by more than expected. The consumer price index rose 0.6% from a month earlier while a key measure of underlying price pressures, which excludes food and energy, was up 0.3%. "This is either a sort of break from the downtrend or a blip," Hassett said in the interview. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh last week did nothing to dispel market expectations that the central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month. In a moderated discussion at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Warsh made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. Hassett said he respects the central bank's independence and said Warsh will "do what he thinks is the right thing." ... "People are really euphoric about how well the economy is doing, and they're spending more. And of course, that's the kind of thing the Fed needs to pay attention to," Hassett said.

items.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq climb as AI-linked stocks recover ahead of earnings By Reuters
items.excerpt: Oct 19 (Reuters) - The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street with a 1% advance on Monday as investors returned to the chip sector and other AI-related stocks following last week’s bruising selloff, while investors waited for key corporate earnings reports. On Friday, the benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq had marked their biggest weekly declines since late June. Concerns that higher interest rates could curb investments in AI infrastructure have been weighing on technology stocks, particularly chip companies and data center operators. The selloff reflected mounting investor unease over how costly AI developments will be financed, a question that has increasingly pressured companies underpinning the US bull market, which recently marked its fourth anniversary. ... The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 36.38 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.03, the S&P 500 gained 31.29 points, or 0.41%, to 7,690.73 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89. However, the market leaned massively on heavyweight stocks for its advance. Also during the session, the indexes had pulled away from their peaks for the day. One issue was that energy markets removed some earlier support as oil prices fluctuated. ... US crude oil futures reversed earlier losses to settle up 2.2% at $103.66 a barrel after attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities. items.title: Stock market news for Oct. 19, 2026
items.excerpt: U.S. homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level since June 2012 in October, as rising mortgage rates, energy and material costs, and worsening labor and lot conditions continue to weigh on housing demand. The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) and Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) dropped three points to 29 in October, its lowest reading since June 2012. The index remains well below the key 50-point threshold that signals positive sentiment. "Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges," said NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz. Dietz said that while demand persists, higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.
